title: Discounts and Marked Price
tagline: Year 2 — Marked price, discount, successive discounts and mark-up

introduction.overview: Shops print a marked price (MP) on goods and then offer a discount, so the selling price (SP) is lower than the marked price. The discount is always a percentage of the marked price, while profit and loss are percentages of the cost price. This chapter combines the two ideas: how much should an item be marked so that after a discount the shopkeeper still earns the target profit?
introduction.placementRelevance: Discount and marked price questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, often as a mark-up followed by one or two successive discounts.
introduction.realWorldContext: Festival sales, "buy 2 get 1 free" offers and coupon discounts are all discount calculations.

learningObjectives: Compute selling price, marked price and discount from each other
Combine mark-up and discount to find the profit or loss
Use successive discounts and the single equivalent discount
Interpret "buy x get y free" offers as discounts
Find the mark-up needed for a target profit

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: SP = MP × (1 − d/100); SP = CP × (1 ± p/100). A multiplier of 0.8 stands for a 20% discount.

coreDefinitions: Marked price (list price): the price printed on the article.
Discount: the reduction given on the marked price. Discount % = (MP − SP) ÷ MP × 100.
Successive discounts: discounts given one after another, each on the reduced price.
Mark-up: the percentage added to the cost price to fix the marked price.
Single equivalent discount: one discount that has the same effect as two or more successive discounts.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Discount works on the marked price; profit works on the cost price. Chains of mark-up and discount are chains of multipliers, so the final price is CP × (mark-up multiplier) × (discount multiplier).
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Set CP = 100. A 40% mark-up gives MP 140. A 20% discount gives SP 112. Profit 12%. This "assume 100" method works for any percentage chain.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Selling price after discount
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Discount is on the marked price.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Buy x get y free
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The free items are the discount.

mainNarrative: To compute the selling price, multiply the marked price by (1 − d/100). If an article marked ₹1,000 is sold at 20% discount the SP is ₹800. To go backwards, divide: SP ₹720 after 10% discount means MP = 720 ÷ 0.9 = ₹800.
Mark-up and discount combine as a chain of multipliers. A shopkeeper who marks goods 40% above cost and gives a 20% discount sells at 1.4 × 0.8 = 1.12 times the cost, which is a 12% profit.
Successive discounts are not additive. 20% followed by 10% is 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, a single discount of 28%, not 30%. The order does not matter for the final price.
To fix the marked price for a target profit, work backwards. For 20% profit with a 10% discount on CP ₹900: MP × 0.9 = 900 × 1.2, so MP = ₹1,200.
Offers like "buy 2 get 1 free" give 1 free item for every 3 taken, which is a discount of 1/3 = 33.3%.

deepDiveAspects.title: Discount is not profit
deepDiveAspects.content: A 20% discount can still leave a profit if the mark-up was high enough. Always compare the final SP with the cost price, not with the marked price.

deepDiveAspects.title: Order of discounts
deepDiveAspects.content: Multiplication is commutative: 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.8 × 0.9. The single equivalent is the same whichever discount is applied first.

solvedExamples.title: Mark-up and discount
solvedExamples.question: A shopkeeper marks goods 40% above the cost price and gives a 20% discount. Find his profit percentage.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The discount is on MP, not CP.

solvedExamples.title: Single equivalent discount
solvedExamples.question: Two successive discounts of 10% and 5% are given on ₹2,000. Find the final price and the single equivalent discount.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The second discount is on the reduced price.

solvedExamples.title: Find the marked price
solvedExamples.question: A dealer buys an article for ₹900. He wants a profit of 20% after allowing a 10% discount. At what price should he mark it?

shortcutMethods.title: Assume cost price 100

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Work in rupees with the given numbers throughout.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Set CP = 100 (or MP = 100), apply each percentage as a multiplier and read the answer as a percentage.

rulesForApplication: Discount on MP, profit on CP.
Buy x get y free → y/(x+y).
To find MP, divide SP by (1 − d).

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Using y/x instead of y/(x + y).
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: The free items are part of the total.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Profit after mark-up and discount must be (mark-up multiplier × discount multiplier) − 1; test this on options.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Use the assume-100 method for percentage chain questions.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: This chapter prepares you for successive percentage questions.

summaryBullets: Buy x get y free: y/(x+y).

Can I find the single equivalent of two discounts?
